**Yes.** The story's central turn, the mother's sunstroke, is foreshadowed throughout. It is set up by the June heat, her stubborn devotion to the garden, the gutter and the father's absence, and the pills the narrator "could not look at directly." So when Doris calls, the event feels fitting rather than arbitrary.

The story also subverts the reader's expectations. The narrator's line about "a month is not a long time" primes us for an elegy and a death. Instead the mother survives, still quarreling about carrot-less Jell-O. That turn is both surprising and true to her character.

The emotional turn works the same way. The narrator reframes the repeated stories and rituals as "maintenance" rather than nostalgia. This grows organically from the earlier image of the stones passed back and forth. The discovered objects (the grocery list, the photo, the mason jars) reward the reader's attention in hindsight. The surprises arise from established details rather than breaking the story's logic.
